title: Tunable Mpemba effect in a polymer-bead system with inertia
authors: Hosung Kwak, Yongjoo Baek, Hawoong Jeong
abstract: We propose an experimentally motivated model in which the Mpemba effect can be controlled through the system's inertia. The model describes a polymer undergoing a denaturation transition whose force-extension curve contains a plateau that slows relaxation. When the system is initially prepared at a higher temperature or under a weaker stretching force, the bead accumulates greater kinetic energy, allowing it to cross the plateau more rapidly and thereby producing the Mpemba effect. Increasing the bead mass broadens the range of initial temperatures over which this mechanism operates. A similar mechanism also generates the inverse Mpemba effect.
summary: The paper models the Mpemba effect in a polymer-bead system by coupling underdamped bead dynamics to the polymer's force landscape. It demonstrates that the bead's inertia (mass) acts as a control parameter, allowing researchers to tune the anomalous relaxation time through kinetic energy accumulation across structural plateaus. This provides a theoretical framework for understanding how initial conditions dictate relaxation rates in complex soft matter systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the Mpemba effect—an anomalous relaxation phenomenon where initial conditions lead to faster relaxation times—and proposes that system inertia can control this effect.
main_result: Inertia, controlled by bead mass, provides a tunable mechanism for observing the Mpemba effect in polymer dynamics; larger masses allow the bead to retain kinetic energy memory across force plateaus, accelerating relaxation.
method: The authors use numerical simulations solving an underdamped Langevin equation coupled to a polymer's force-extension relation, analyzing time evolution after thermal or mechanical quenches.
model_or_system: The system models a point mass (bead) attached to a polymer (like DNA) undergoing denaturation. The dynamics are governed by the bead's underdamped motion coupled to the polymer's force landscape, which features a plateau regime.
key_observables: Relaxation time ($\tau_{\text{relax}}$), kinetic energy $\langle K(t) \rangle$, and mean extension $\langle x(t) \rangle$ as functions of initial temperature ($T_0$) or force quench magnitude.
important_parameters: Bead mass ($m$), initial temperature ($T_0$), applied external force ($f_{\text{ex}}$), and the operational definition of the plateau regime ($|df_{\text{poly}}/dx| < 0.05$).
main_assumptions: The polymer is assumed to follow an equilibrium force–extension relation even during non-equilibrium bead motion, and hydrodynamic memory effects are neglected.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate the Mpemba effect via overtaking relaxation curves (Fig. 1(c)) and show how $\tau_{\text{relax}}$ exhibits nonmonotonicity with $T_0$ for different bead masses.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model using a Langevin equation, details simulation protocols involving equilibration and quenching, analyzes the role of inertia (mass) in controlling relaxation dynamics across force plateaus, and compares thermal vs. mechanical quench mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work connects non-equilibrium statistical mechanics concepts (like anomalous relaxation) to mesoscopic physical systems (polymers), offering a clear, tunable mechanism based on inertial effects that could be relevant for understanding complex biological or soft matter dynamics.

Figure 2. Simulation results demonstrating the Mpemba effect induced by a point mass attached to an overstretched DNA. Relaxation times trelax (a) for a temperature quench from T0 to T1 = 0.4 with fixed fex = 0.76 and (b) for a force quench from f0 to f1 = 0.76 with fixed T = 0.4 are shown for different masses m. The ranges of T0 and f0 exhibiting the Mpemba effect are highlighted by horizontal arrows. We also show contributions of (c) the pre-plateau regime and (d) the plateau regime to trelax after the temperature quench shown in (a). Lines are to guide the eye, and shaded bands represent the 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
